clinicalPearls: Maternal uniparental disomy 15 is one mechanism of Prader-Willi syndrome, since two maternal copies mean absent paternal expression at 15q11-q13, and it accounts for roughly a quarter of cases
Prader-Willi syndrome presents in infancy with profound hypotonia, poor suck, and feeding difficulty or failure to thrive
In early childhood the picture switches to hyperphagia and progressive obesity if intake is not controlled
Hypogonadism, short stature from growth-hormone deficiency, small hands and feet, and a characteristic facial appearance are typical
Intellectual disability is usually mild-to-moderate, with behavioural difficulties and a characteristic temper and obsessive profile
The UPD subtype carries a lower recurrence risk than an imprinting defect but a slightly higher reported rate of autism spectrum disorder and psychosis than the deletion subtype
Maternal UPD15 typically arises via trisomy 15 rescue, so it is associated with advanced maternal age and confined placental mosaicism
reference.pathophysiology: The Prader-Willi region at 15q11-q13 contains paternally expressed genes that are silenced on the maternal chromosome. In maternal uniparental disomy 15 both chromosome 15s come from the mother, so there is no paternal contribution and the paternally expressed genes are not transcribed, producing Prader-Willi syndrome. This uniparental disomy most often results from rescue of an initial trisomy 15 through loss of the paternal chromosome, which is why it is associated with advanced maternal age; the same clinical picture can also follow a paternal deletion or an imprinting defect.
additionalDifferentials: Deletion or imprinting-defect Prader-Willi syndrome, the same phenotype with a different mechanism
Other causes of neonatal hypotonia, whether neuromuscular or central
Other syndromic obesity such as Bardet-Biedl and Cohen syndromes
Angelman syndrome, the reciprocal disorder of paternal UPD15
Hypothalamic or acquired causes of hyperphagia and obesity
additionalInvestigations: Methylation analysis of the 15q11-q13 locus as the first-line test, abnormal in all Prader-Willi syndrome regardless of mechanism
Follow-up testing by microsatellite or SNP analysis, FISH, and microarray to distinguish maternal disomy from deletion or imprinting defect
Chromosomal microarray, which detects deletions but not uniparental disomy
Growth and endocrine assessment for growth-hormone status and hypogonadism
redFlags: Severe neonatal hypotonia with respiratory or feeding compromise
Rapid weight gain with complications of morbid obesity
A behavioural or psychiatric crisis, given the higher psychosis risk in the disomy subtype
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, growth-hormone therapy, and strict dietary and behavioural management, outcomes have improved, but morbid obesity and its complications remain the main threat to health and life expectancy, and a higher rate of psychiatric illness is noted in the uniparental disomy subtype.
pitfalls: Relying on microarray or FISH, which detect deletions but miss uniparental disomy, when a methylation test is needed first
Not subtyping after a positive methylation test, which affects recurrence-risk counselling
Missing the infantile diagnosis because early hypotonia is non-specific
Underestimating the raised psychiatric risk in maternal UPD15 cases
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Cassidy and Allanson's Management of Genetic Syndromes
management: Growth hormone replacement therapy to improve stature, body composition and muscle tone
Strict lifelong dietary energy restriction with a supervised, controlled food environment to prevent hyperphagia-driven obesity
Sex hormone replacement for hypogonadism and to support pubertal development and bone health
Early physiotherapy and feeding support for the infantile hypotonia, poor suck and failure to thrive
Behavioural and psychological or psychiatric support, with heightened vigilance for autism spectrum disorder and psychosis in the uniparental disomy subtype
Surveillance for obesity-related complications including obstructive sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes and scoliosis
Genetic counselling noting the lower recurrence risk of the uniparental disomy subtype compared with an imprinting defect
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across endocrinology, dietetics, genetics and developmental and behavioural services
